Key Topic 1 Chronological Enquiry Sequence • c1250–c1500

Medicine in Medieval Britain, c1250–c1500

c1250–c1500: Ideas on Causes, Prevention, Treatment, Medical Care & The Black Death
Historical Primary Record • c.1350 MS 13076 • FOLIO 24V
Omne Bonum: Clerics Ministering to Plague Victims with Buboes
James le Palmer (fl. 1360–1375) • Fourteenth-century illuminated manuscript showing two plague sufferers bearing bubonic sores in bed while priests administer last rites and prayer.
Primary Visual Evidence The British Library Manuscript Collection
Pearson Edexcel Option 11 • Key Topic 1 Content
Official Specification Directory
1 Ideas About the Cause of Disease and Illness
▪ Supernatural and religious explanations of the cause of disease.
▪ Rational explanations: the Theory of the Four Humours and the miasma theory; the continuing influence in England of Galen.
2 Approaches to Prevention and Treatment
▪ Approaches to prevention and treatment, and their connection with ideas about disease and illness: religious actions, bloodletting and purging, purifying the air.
▪ Medical training and traditional approaches to treatment and care for the sick: the role of the physician, apothecary and barber surgeon; the role of hospitals, care within the community and at home, including the use of herbal remedies.
3 Case Study
▪ Dealing with the Black Death, 1348–49; approaches to treatment and attempts to prevent its spread.
🎯 Case Study Depth Focus National & Local Dimensions: Contrasting supernatural beliefs (divine wrath, flagellants) and humoral purging against King Edward III’s 1349 cleanliness order and London quarantine pits.

Q3 • 4 MARKS AO1/AO2 Concept Drill
Similarity or Difference Across Eras
Target: Explain 1 way [ideas / treatments / care] in this era were similar or different to another period.
Rule: Provide specific factual evidence from both named periods to secure 4/4 marks (approx. 5 mins).
Practice: In-Workbook 4-Mark Comparative Tasks
Q4 • 12 MARKS AO1/AO2 Causation
Explain Why [Causal Change] Occurred
Target: Multi-causal analytical essay explaining why medical change or continuity took place.
Rule: Write 3 developed PEEL paragraphs. Must address both stimulus points + 1 distinct point of own knowledge (18 mins).
Practice: Chronological Inquiry Spine & Causation Drills
Q5/6 • 16+4 SPaG AO1/AO2/AO4 Synoptic
‘How Far Do You Agree?’ Evaluative Essay
Target: Choose Q5 OR Q6. Evaluative thematic essay assessing factor significance or change over time.
Rule: Balanced argument (for/against) with sustained criteria and a decisive historical verdict (30 mins).
Practice: Full 16-Mark Extended Writing Frames

King Edward III ordered Londoners to clean human filth off the streets in 1349. Outstanding for civic smell, totally useless against Yersinia pestis fleas. 3/20
KEY TOPIC 1.1 • LESSON NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 (1HI0/11)

Why did the Catholic Church dominate medieval explanations of disease?

Audio • Quiz
1 c1250–1500• Why did medieval Christians view epidemic disease as punishment from God?
2 c1250–1500• How did Biblical moral stigma shape the treatment of medieval lepers?
3 1345• How did physicians use Zodiac Man charts and the 1345 alignment?
4 c1350• Why did sick people turn to pilgrimage shrines rather than doctors?
5 c1400• Why did church enforcement of Galen prevent medical progress?
4/20 If you develop a fever in 1300, church logic dictates you definitely committed a sin last Tuesday. Time to buy a pilgrimage badge!

Question 5: Evaluative Essay [16 marks + 4 marks SPaG • 25 mins]

Extended Writing Assessment
‘In the medieval period (c1250–c1500), ideas about the cause of illness were mainly based on religion.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer. [16 marks + 4 marks SPaG]
Stimulus: the Church miasma (You must also use information of your own)
Analytical Connectives: To a large extent, it can be argued that... • On the one hand, a major religious belief was that... • Furthermore, this meant that... • On the other hand, an alternative rational explanation was... • In conclusion, the decisive reason why...
Write your response in the space provided below: (Response continues on facing page)
Mind-Map Mission Open the Consolidate Station in the app and branch out KT1.1 on Pages 2–3: map Church manuscript control and Roger Bacon’s arrest (left) against pilgrimage and prayer (right).
[    ] Done
Galen wrote it, monks copied it, nobody dared question it. Because questioning Galen wasn’t just bad science—it was a heresy trial. 5/20

KEY TOPIC 1.2 • LESSON NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 (1HI0/11)

Why did the Theory of the Four Humours dominate rational medicine for centuries?

Audio • Quiz
1 c460 BC• How did Hippocrates separate medicine from superstition?
2 c1250• Why did humoral theory seem logical to medieval people?
3 c1280• How did the Theory of Opposites provide practical treatment rules?
4 c1300• Why did uroscopy give physicians great diagnostic authority?
5 c1350• Why did rational physicians link bad smells directly to epidemics?
Cold and wet? Have some hot dry pepper. Too much blood? Let’s slice your arm open. Galen’s logic was flawless, provided you survived the cure. 7/20

Analytical Connectives: One main reason was that... • For example, ... • This was important because... • Another key factor was... • In particular, ... • Overall, the most decisive reason was... because...

8/20 Sniffing urine, tasting urine, holding urine up to the window. 14th-century diagnostics was 90% liquid inspection and 10% guessing.

Explain the logic: the Theory of Opposites provided clear, practical action for every physician, even when the patient grew worse. 9/20
KEY TOPIC 1.3 • LESSON NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 (1HI0/11)

How did medieval people attempt to treat and prevent disease, and why did rational and religious methods coexist?

Audio • Quiz
1 c1250• Why did ordinary people consider prayer more vital than medicine?
2 c1300• Why was bloodletting the most universal physical treatment?
3 c1320• How was purging believed to restore bodily equilibrium?
4 c1350• Why did herbal recipes remain popular across all social classes?
5 c1400• How did wealthy barons attempt to prevent sickness before it struck?
10/20 Bleeding, purging, boiling vinegar, and swallowing crushed emeralds. If the disease didn’t kill you, the apothecary’s bill definitely would.

KEY TOPIC 1.4 • LESSON NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 (1HI0/11)

Who provided medical care in medieval England, and why did hospitals focus on care rather than cure?

Audio • Quiz
1 c1250• Why were university physicians accessible only to the ultra-wealthy?
2 c1300• How did apothecaries provide accessible medicines to townspeople?
3 c1320• Why were barber-surgeons viewed as lower-status craftsmen?
4 c1350• Why did monastic hospitals deliberately avoid medical treatment?
5 c1400• Why did the vast majority of sick people rely on female family members?
Medieval hospitals: clean sheets, warm porridge, 24-hour prayer, and absolutely zero doctors. It was luxury hospitality, not clinical medicine. 13/20

KEY TOPIC 1.5 • LESSON NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 (1HI0/11)

Why did medieval society fail to halt the devastating mortality of the Black Death?

Audio • Quiz
1 June 1348• How did trade routes unwittingly bring the plague to England?
2 Autumn 1348• Why was the pneumonic strain far deadlier than the bubonic form?
3 Winter 1348• Why were medical treatments completely useless against the plague?
4 1349• How did belief in miasma shape royal prevention orders?
5 1349–1350• How did losing a third of England’s people weaken feudal serfdom?
16/20 In 1348, people blamed God, the planets, bad smells, and foreigners. The actual culprits—fleas on black rats—went completely unnoticed.
